Closing gaps and cracks in a home’s shell so heated or cooled air cannot leak out. Usually the cheapest, highest-payback efficiency upgrade.
A heat pump that moves heat between outdoor air and your home. Works for heating and cooling, including in cold climates with modern models.
Annual Fuel Utilization Efficiency: the share of a furnace or boiler’s fuel that becomes useful heat. A 95% AFUE furnace wastes 5%.
The electricity your home uses all the time, day and night, from fridges, routers and devices on standby.
A home battery that stores electricity from solar or the grid for later use or backup during outages.
Able to be broken down by microorganisms. Without a timeframe and conditions, the label means little.
A professional test that depressurises a home with a fan to measure how leaky it is and find air leaks.
British thermal unit, a unit of heat energy. 1 kWh is about 3,412 BTU.
The total greenhouse gas emissions caused by a person, household, product or organisation, usually in tonnes of CO₂e per year.
A credit representing a tonne of emissions reduced or removed elsewhere. Quality varies widely, so reducing your own emissions comes first.
Carbon dioxide equivalent: a way to express different greenhouse gases as the amount of CO₂ that would cause the same warming.
A shared solar farm that households subscribe to for a bill credit, without panels on their own roof.
Decomposed organic matter used to improve soil. Composting food scraps keeps them out of landfills, where they would release methane.
Coefficient of performance: units of heat a heat pump delivers per unit of electricity. A COP of 3 means 3 kWh of heat for 1 kWh of electricity.
A charge based on your highest burst of power use in a billing period, measured in kW.
The share of a solar system’s rated output that actually reaches your home after losses from heat, wiring, inverters and dirt.
A heat pump with indoor wall or ceiling units connected to an outdoor unit, needing no ducts.
Emissions from making, transporting and installing a product or building, as opposed to running it.
An assessment of where a home wastes energy, done yourself or by a professional with diagnostic tools.
Canada’s official rating of home energy performance, used by federal and provincial retrofit programs.
A US EPA program certifying products and homes that meet energy-efficiency specifications.
Electric vehicle, powered by a battery charged from the grid rather than by burning fuel.
The rate your utility or supplier pays for solar power you send to the grid. Also called a feed-in tariff or export credit.
A payment per kWh for electricity a home generates and sends to the grid.
A ground-source heat pump that moves heat between your home and the ground through buried pipes.
Marketing that makes a product or company seem more environmentally friendly than it is.
The average kilograms of CO₂ released per kWh of electricity on a given grid. Clean grids are near zero; coal-heavy grids are high.
A water heater that uses heat pump technology, typically using a fraction of the electricity of a standard electric tank.
A US home energy rating score; lower numbers mean a more efficient home.
An electric cooktop that heats pans directly with a magnetic field. Fast, efficient and free of combustion fumes.
The device that converts solar panels’ direct current (DC) into alternating current (AC) for your home.
Kilowatt: a unit of power, the rate of energy use or production at a moment.
Kilowatt-hour: a unit of energy. Running a 1,000-watt appliance for an hour uses 1 kWh.
A 240-volt home EV charger that adds roughly 30–50 km of range per hour.
Window glass with a thin coating that reflects heat, keeping homes warmer in winter and cooler in summer.
Microgeneration Certification Scheme: the UK standard installers must meet for heat pumps and solar to qualify for grants.
A greenhouse gas far more potent than CO₂ over the short term, released by landfills, livestock and gas leaks.
A billing arrangement where solar power you export offsets power you buy, usually at the full retail rate.
A state where greenhouse gas emissions released are balanced by those removed from the atmosphere.
Hours when electricity demand and often prices are lower, usually overnight.
How long it takes for an upgrade’s savings to equal its upfront cost.
The equivalent number of hours per day of full-strength sunlight a location receives. Used to estimate solar output.
Electricity drawn by devices that are switched off or on standby. Also called standby or vampire power.
Power purchase agreement: a company installs and owns solar on your roof and sells you the power at an agreed rate.
A measure of insulation’s resistance to heat flow. Higher is better.
Money returned after buying or installing a qualifying product, from a government, utility or manufacturer.
Energy from sources that are naturally replenished, such as sun, wind, water and geothermal heat.
Seasonal Energy Efficiency Ratio: a US rating of air conditioner and heat pump cooling efficiency.
A thermostat that learns schedules or adjusts automatically to cut heating and cooling when you are out or asleep.
An electricity tariff with different prices at different times of day.
A measure of how much heat passes through a material or window. Lower is better. The inverse of R-value.
Turning waste or unwanted items into something of higher value or use.
Composting with worms, which turn food scraps into nutrient-rich castings. Works indoors.
Strips of material that seal gaps around doors and windows.
An approach that aims to send nothing to landfill by refusing, reducing, reusing, recycling and composting.
